resources.string: Produced on your phone. Nothing about signing in reaches anyone else, and no outage elsewhere can stop it.
A public Anisette server does it for you. Its operator can see that traffic, and sign-in stops working when their server does.
You will have to sign in again. Apple ties a session to whatever produced its sign-in data, so changing this looks like a new device.
Sets itself up the next time you sign in
Apple has replaced the file this needs, so it can no longer set itself up. You can supply a copy of %1$s yourself, or use a remote server instead.
That file is not the version this needs (%1$s).
Your phone can now do this itself, instead of going through a public Anisette server that sees the traffic and takes sign-in down with it. Switching costs one sign-in.
You can switch later in Settings.
This device could not set up sign-in on its own, so a server has to do it this time. You can change this later in Settings.
Color the app from your wallpaper. Needs Android 12 or later.
Are you sure you want to remove these devices? Once removed they will need to be reimported to get them back.
That file is not a zip. Choose the zip file the OpenTagViewer exporter made.
This zip was not made by the OpenTagViewer exporter, so there is nothing to import.
This export could not be read. It may be incomplete, or made by a newer version of the exporter.
This export does not contain any tags, so there is nothing to import.
That file could not be opened. Choose it again.
Enter the code the exporter showed when it made this file. Capital letters, spaces and dashes do not matter.
That code did not open the bundle. Check it against the one the exporter showed.
This bundle is locked and no code was entered.
A code is made of digits and letters only.

Apple no longer accepts the saved sign-in for this device, so your tags cannot be located until you sign in again.
Your tags and their location history stay on this phone — nothing has been lost.
An OpenHaystack-style tag. Its keys were generated by whoever made it and were never in an Apple account, so it has no name, emoji or battery level from Apple — set your own below.
Could not reach Apple. Check your connection and try again.
Your password was accepted, but Apple is waiting for you to agree to these terms before the account can be used. They are shown in full below — this is what you would be agreeing to.
Apple gave no way to record agreement to this document, so it cannot be accepted here. Signing in at icloud.com may work instead.
Signing in got as far as your account and then stopped. If that is about terms of service, they can be shown and accepted here. If it is about something else, accepting terms will not fix it.
Fetch my tags from my Apple account
This needs the screen-lock passcode of one of your Apple devices — its PIN or login password, not your Apple ID password.
Which device’s passcode do you have?
That was not accepted. It is worth trying the same passcode again — this check sometimes fails and then works.
No tags owned by this account
Tags are registered by an iPhone or iPad, and only that account can unlock them. This account has no device that can.
If a friend shared their tags with you in Find My, that sharing does not include the keys this app needs. Ask them to export a bundle for you, and import it here.
Could not check your account just now
Apple reported nothing usable at all, which usually means the service is having a bad day rather than anything being wrong with your account. Worth trying again later.
Found %1$d tags in your Apple account
%1$d other items on this account carry no location key, so nothing can find them.
Read my tags from my Apple account
Turning this off stops reading your tag list. It does not remove OpenTagViewer from your Apple device list — that is yours to do in Apple’s own settings.
What is on your Apple account
Show your friend how to export
Looking for a device that can unlock it…
This tag comes from your Apple account, so the app only holds a copy of it. Remove it in Find My on an Apple device, and it will go from here the next time the app reads your account.
These tags come from your Apple account, so the app only holds copies of them. Remove them in Find My on an Apple device, and they will go from here the next time the app reads your account.
%1$d of these came from your Apple account and will stay — remove those in Find My on an Apple device. The rest will be removed from this app.
%1$s is a Bluetooth SIG company identifier. Tap to look it up and find out who made this.
This tag is named in your Apple account, so renaming it has to reach Apple — and that did not work just now. Nothing has changed. Check your connection and try again.
Add the tags on your account, or update the ones already here
Linked to your Apple account. Tap to check for new or changed tags.
No updates for months — paused checking
Backing off — %1$d empty searches, next attempt %2$s
Ignored since %1$s — nothing found across months of history

Nothing has been found for this tag anywhere in months of history, so the app stopped searching for it automatically. Searching for one of these is slow, and it is unlikely to be found. Tap below to look again right now.
Looking for this tag again. This can take a few minutes.
Only tags read from iCloud ever update this. A tag imported from a file keeps whatever value it had when the export was made.
Stop this app reading tags from your account

This app will stop reading your tags from Apple. Tags you have already imported stay on this device, along with their location history — but they will no longer be updated from your account.
This does not remove this app from your Apple account. To do that, open Find My on an Apple device and remove it there.
You can link again later. That needs your Apple device passcode.
Your Apple account is no longer linked
Could not unlink your Apple account. Please try again.
No app on this phone can open a map
Waiting for the location check to finish…
Log file has been exported successfully
Could not export the log file

Your iPhones, iPads and Macs can only be located here through the Find My network, the same way an AirTag is. That means they update rarely and unpredictably, unlike Apple\'s own app, which reads the position a device reports to iCloud itself. Off by default because that coverage is fundamentally incomplete. While off, these devices are neither shown nor searched for.
No app on this phone can open a web link
Your session is still signed in, but Apple has asked for a code again. Enter it to carry on — nothing can be located until you do.
That code was not accepted. %1$d attempts left.
That code was not accepted. Signing out — you will need to sign in again.

This app can connect to your Apple account and read your tags from it directly. New tags show up on their own, renaming one writes it back, and there is no zip to export from a Mac.
You can set this up now, or any time later from Settings.
This app is a device on your Apple account

Do not remove this entry.

Apple shows it beside “If you do not recognise this device”, so it looks like something to tidy up. Removing it stops this app reading your tags — at best you will have to sign in and enter a verification code again, and it can sign you out completely.

Apple names the entry itself, so the serial ^1 is the only thing that tells it apart from a real Mac. Every fresh install adds another one.
%1$s lists this app as one of your devices:

Something came back that this app does not know how to read, so retrying will not help and there is nothing to change in your settings.\n\nThat usually means Apple altered something. A report with the log attached is what makes it fixable — the log almost always says which part.
Opens GitHub, which will ask you to sign in or create an account first.
The log is cleaned before it leaves the app: %1$s
The log cannot be shared right now, because the part of the app that removes personal details from it is not running. Reporting without it still helps.

The app could not read that file, and cannot say what is wrong with it — so trying again with the same file will not help.\n\nIf it came from the exporter it should have worked, which makes this worth reporting. The log usually says which part it stopped on.

They are saved on this phone and will stay there. What did not work was asking Apple where they are:

%1$s

That is usually the Anisette server your sign-in goes through — when a public one is down, locations stop arriving while everything else looks fine. Producing sign-in data on this device instead avoids depending on anyone else’s server.

The app keeps trying every minute, so a brief outage sorts itself out.
How do you want the log?
Copy it, to paste into the report
Save it as a file, to attach
The log could not be saved, because the part of the app that removes personal details from it is not running. Nothing was written — an uncleaned log is not worth handing out.
Log saved. It was cleaned first: %1$s

The person you send this file to needs the code below to open it.\n\nSend it to them separately — a code sent in the same message as the file is in the same place as the file, and anyone who has both can locate these tags until you unpair them.
This code is not stored anywhere and cannot be shown again.
“%1$s” cannot be exported: this app has no naming record for it, and a bundle without one imports as nothing. Tags read from your Apple account are shared through Find My rather than through a file.
The file could not be written. Nothing was saved.

The app could not build a bundle from the tags you picked, and cannot say why — so trying again with the same tags will not help.\n\nNothing was sent and nothing on this phone has changed. Your tags are still here.
No tags imported from a file
Up to date with your Apple account
Could not reach your Apple account just now. Your tags are unchanged.
This log is too large to copy. Save it as a file and attach that instead.
Not found nearby. Move closer and try again.
Connected, but this accessory has no sound service.
Could not compute this accessory\'s current address.
Bluetooth permission is needed to play the sound nearby.
Could not play the sound. Try again.
Read from the tag over Bluetooth just now, not from iCloud.
Listens for your tags even when the app is closed, and records where they were heard. Needs a permanent notification, and uses more battery. Off by default.
Shown while the app is listening for your tags in the background.
Alerts you when a tag stops being heard and you have moved away from it.
Last heard where you were %1$s. Tap to see the place.
Sounds an alarm when this tag stops being heard and you have moved on. Needs background listening to be on.
How long a tag has to go unheard before the app decides you have left it behind. It listens at full power from halfway through that time, so a shorter wait warns you sooner and costs more battery.

This app has a connection to your Apple account saved, but can no longer read it. The keys it needs are kept in this device\'s secure storage, and they cannot be recovered — so the connection has to be made again.
Your tags and their location history are not affected, and nothing was removed from your Apple account.
The saved Apple account connection could not be decrypted, although its key is still present

The connection to your Apple account is stored on this device, the key that unlocks it is still here, and it no longer opens — which should not be possible.\n\nThat makes it worth reporting rather than just redoing. Your tags and their location history are not affected, and nothing was removed from your Apple account.
None stored — the next fetch searches from the pairing date
Apple accepted your code and then had a problem finishing the sign-in. The code is used up, so a new one is needed — waiting a moment before asking for it, because asking straight away is refused.
Asking Apple for a new code in %1$d s…

Apple is still not finishing the sign-in. This is a fault on Apple\'s side, not something you did, and not your code.\n\nTry again in a few minutes. Your password may be refused once when you do — that is part of the same fault, so enter it again rather than assuming it is wrong.

Apple refused the sign-in. This is Apple declining, not a problem with your Apple ID or password. Trying again shortly is worth doing, but if it keeps refusing please report it with a log rather than waiting it out.
Apple is not answering right now
Apple refused the request rather than failing to answer it. Nothing is wrong with your account, and nothing was changed. Try again shortly; if it keeps refusing, report it with a log.

Import the missing tags first, then import this history ZIP again to restore the skipped rows.
This export does not identify tags safely, so its history cannot be restored. Create a new Export History ZIP with the current app and import that file instead.
Choose an undamaged ZIP created by Export History in OpenTagViewer for Android.
No history was imported. Try again, or choose another Export History ZIP.

The app could not restore history from the file you picked, and cannot say why — so trying again with the same file may not help.
No history was imported and nothing already stored was changed.

Signing in did not get through. The log below says which step failed and what came back, which is almost always the part that explains it.
If Apple simply refused the request, waiting and trying again is worth doing first. If it keeps failing, a report with this log attached is what makes it fixable.
Apple refused the sign-in and asked for %1$s before trying again. This is Apple declining, not a problem with your Apple ID or password.

Your password and code were accepted, and then Apple would not open iCloud for this account. This is not about terms of service. Other apps that sign in this way see it on Apple IDs that have never been used with an Apple device, and signing in at appleid.apple.com and completing the account details — adding a payment method, for instance — is what usually clears it. Waiting on its own generally does not.
Apple\'s sign-in library crashes on this phone, so a server does this step instead. Everything else works normally. We don\'t know why it happens on some phones yet, and a report naming yours helps.

Apple\'s sign-in library crashes as soon as it loads on this phone. It works on most phones, and we do not know yet what the affected ones have in common.\n\nOpenTagViewer now uses a server for that step, so you can sign in and use the app normally. A report with the details below is what helps us find the cause.

Apple refused to start signing in to this Apple ID before your password was checked, so retyping it will not help. Check that you can sign in at account.apple.com and whether Apple asks anything of you there. Trying a remote server presents Apple with a different device, which is worth a try. Apple said: %1$s
Experimental. Locate the trackers in your Google account through your own googlefind service. They can be added as devices, or linked to a device so both networks\' reports show on one marker.
